name: St Mary's Church, Garforth
text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church, on the train's {side}, completed in 1844 to a design by George Fowler Jones. Built of dressed magnesian limestone, it is cross-shaped, with a tower and broach spire over the crossing.

name: Austhorpe Hall
text: Your train passes near Austhorpe Hall, on the train's {side}, a red-brick house of 1694 with a Baroque doorway under a triangular pediment, which Pevsner called a remarkably early case of the classical style being taken up. In 1740 a coal mine on its estate was given an early Newcomen steam engine, only the fourth to be built.

name: Leeds Corn Exchange
text: Your train passes near the Leeds Corn Exchange, on the train's {side}, an oval building by Cuthbert Brodrick, the architect of Leeds Town Hall, completed in 1863. Its dome was modelled on the Halle aux blés in Paris; once a corn market, it is now a Grade I listed home for independent shops.

name: Round Foundry
text: Your train passes near the Round Foundry, on the train's {side}, built in 1795 to 1797 by Fenton, Murray and Wood. Here Matthew Murray made textile machinery, steam engines and the first locomotives for the Middleton Railway, among them Salamanca, and it grew into one of the world's first specialist engineering foundries.

name: Stank Hall Barn
text: Your train passes Stank Hall Barn, on the train's {side}, a Grade II* barn of the late 15th century built for the Beeston family. Beside it stands Stank Old Hall, from the 13th century, which was built as a royal hunting lodge for nearby Rothwell Castle and still has a rare garderobe, or privy.

name: HM Prison Wakefield
text: Your train passes near HM Prison Wakefield, on the train's {side}, which began as a house of correction in 1594, though most of its buildings are Victorian. It is the oldest dispersal prison still working in England and Wales, and "being sent to Wakefield" was once a way of saying being sent to prison.

name: Theatre Royal Wakefield
text: Your train passes near the Theatre Royal, on the train's {side}, designed in 1894 by Frank Matcham and the smallest of his theatres still standing. It closed in 1954 and became a cinema and then a bingo hall, before reopening as a theatre in 1981.

name: County Hall, Wakefield
text: Your train passes near County Hall, on the train's {side}, opened in 1898 as the headquarters of the West Riding County Council, after much debate over whether it should be in Leeds or Wakefield. Listed Grade I, it is now the headquarters of Wakefield Council.

name: Walton
text: Your train passes near Walton, on the train's {side}, a village on the Barnsley Canal. In 1820 the naturalist and explorer Charles Waterton turned the grounds of his home, Walton Hall, into the world's first nature reserve; the hall is now a hotel, and the park is known as Waterton Park.

name: Belle Vue
text: Your train passes near Belle Vue, on the train's {side}, a mile south of Wakefield city centre and the home of the rugby league club Wakefield Trinity, which first played on Heath Common. The football club Wakefield A.F.C. also played here.

name: Kirkthorpe Hydro
text: Your train passes near Kirkthorpe Hydro, on the train's {side}, a hydroelectric plant opened in 2017 on the River Calder at Kirkthorpe Weir, which was built in 1827 and is the highest industrial weir in Yorkshire. With another plant at Brotherton, on the River Aire, it is jointly the largest hydroelectric generator in Yorkshire, and it has passes built in for fish and eels.

name: The Hepworth Wakefield
text: Your train passes near The Hepworth Wakefield, on the train's {side}, an art gallery on the south bank of the River Calder, named after the sculptor Barbara Hepworth, who was born and educated in the city. Designed by David Chipperfield as ten trapezoidal blocks, it opened in 2011 and had more than 500,000 visitors in its first year.

name: Post Office Road
text: Your train passes near Post Office Road, on the train's {side}, the ground of Featherstone Rovers since the club was formed in 1908; the ground itself opened in 1904. Its record crowd, 17,000, came in 1957 for a game against St Helens, and the seats at its Railway End came second-hand from Scarborough's McCain Stadium.

name: Pontefract Barracks
text: Your train passes near the former Pontefract Barracks, on the train's {side}, built in the Gothic Revival style and finished in 1879. From 1881 they were the depot of both the King's Own Yorkshire Light Infantry and the York and Lancaster Regiment; they closed in 1963 and are now offices.

name: Pontefract Castle
text: Your train passes near Pontefract Castle, on the train's {side}, begun in about 1070 by Ilbert de Lacy on land given to him by William the Conqueror. King Richard II is thought to have died here, and the castle was besieged several times during the Civil War.

name: Prince of Wales Colliery
text: Your train passes near the site of the Prince of Wales Colliery, on the train's {side}, a coal mine known locally as the "Ponty Prince", which began producing coal in 1869. It worked for more than 130 years, until geological problems closed it in 2002, and most of the site is now housing.

name: Lagentium
text: Your train passes near the site of Lagentium, on the train's {side}, a Roman fort of turf and timber built around the year 74 to guard the river crossings and the road to the north. The town of Castleford now stands on it.

name: Methley
text: Your train passes near Methley, on the train's {side}, a scattered village near where the rivers Aire and Calder meet. The first village grew up by St Oswald's Church, and its 17th- and 18th-century buildings still stand along Church Side; the name may come from Old English for a mowing wood or clearing.

name: Wakefield Europort
text: Your train passes Wakefield Europort, on the train's {side}, a rail-connected warehousing estate opened in 1996 in readiness for the extra freight expected through the Channel Tunnel. By 2012 it employed more than 3,000 people, and the site of the old Altofts and Whitwood station lies within it.

name: Queen's Mill
text: Your train passes near Queen's Mill, on the train's {side}, on the River Aire, where a watermill was first recorded in 1093. Renamed for Queen Victoria's Golden Jubilee in 1887, it was the first building in the town with electric light, and after Allinson enlarged it in 1979 and 1980 it was the world's largest stoneground flour mill, with 20 pairs of millstones.

name: Wheldon Road
text: Your train passes near Wheldon Road, on the train's {side}, the ground of Castleford Tigers since 1927; it opened a year earlier. Its record crowd of 25,449 came on March 9th 1935, for a Challenge Cup tie against Hunslet.

name: Gascoigne Wood Mine
text: Your train passes near the site of Gascoigne Wood Mine, on the train's {side}, the hub of the Selby coalfield: coal from all its mines came to the surface here before leaving by rail. At its peak, in 1993 to 1994, the coalfield produced 12 million tonnes a year, about 45 per cent of the United Kingdom's deep-mined coal; mining ended in 2004.

name: Ferry Bridge
text: Your train passes near Ferry Bridge, on the train's {side}, which carried the Great North Road over the River Aire. Designed in 1797 by John Carr of York and finished in 1804, it has eight round arches; an earlier bridge here was partly destroyed by the Lancastrian army in 1461, but the Yorkists still crossed on their way to Towton.

name: Monk Fryston Hall
text: Your train passes near Monk Fryston Hall, on the train's {side}, first built in the 13th century for Selby Abbey, in magnesian limestone, and heavily restored in about 1740. The Hemsworth family bought it in 1680 and lived there for several generations; later a hotel, it was sold in 1954 to the 10th Duke of Rutland.

name: St Wilfrid's Church, Monk Fryston
text: Your train passes near St Wilfrid's Church, Monk Fryston, on the train's {side}, the lower part of whose tower survives from the Saxon period, probably the early 11th century. The rest was rebuilt in the 13th and 14th centuries; in the Middle Ages the church was dedicated to Mary, and it is listed Grade I.

name: Corunna House
text: Your train passes near Corunna House, on the train's {side}, a brown-brick house facing the River Ouse, built before 1724 for Richard Pearson. Pevsner called it "the handsomest house in Selby"; it was a school from the 1850s until 1926, and its name comes from a supposed link with John Moore of La Coruña.

name: Pontefract Hermitage
text: Your train passes near the Pontefract Hermitage, on the train's {side}, two chambers cut into the sandstone beneath Southgate, with a steep spiral staircase down to a well cut in the rock. It was given to a hermit, Brother Adam, in 1386, is listed Grade I, and can be visited on open days.

name: Fitzwilliam
text: Your train passes Fitzwilliam, on the train's {side}, a pit village built for the miners of Fitzwilliam Main, a colliery named after its owners' family. The colliery was renamed Hemsworth Colliery and closed in 1969; the village's station closed in 1967 and reopened in 1982.

name: Kinsley
text: Your train passes near Kinsley, on the train's {side}, a former mining village best known for the Kinsley evictions of August 15th 1905, when police turned 25 families out of their homes during a strike at Hemsworth Colliery. Left homeless, the families in the end set up camp at Outwood Hall farm.

name: Hampole Priory
text: Your train passes the site of Hampole Priory, on the train's {side}, a house of Cistercian nuns recorded in a papal bull of 1146, whose nuns were active in the wool trade. The 14th-century mystic Richard Rolle, the "hermit of Hampole", settled here and lived here until his death in 1349; a cottage now stands on the site.

name: Adwick Town Hall
text: Your train passes near Adwick Town Hall, on the train's {side}, built around 1682 as the rectory of St Laurence's Church for the vicar, Joshua Brook, who sank a well and planted an orchard there. It stands in the grounds of Adwick Manor, the seat of the Washington family from the 16th century.

name: Doncaster Minster
text: Your train passes near Doncaster Minster, on the train's {side}, built in 1854 to 1858 to George Gilbert Scott's design after fire destroyed the medieval church in 1853. Pevsner thought it the most cathedral-like of all Scott's parish churches; it has a Schulze organ and a celebrated clock by Dent.

name: Selby Abbey
text: Your train passes near Selby Abbey, on the train's {side}, founded in 1069 by Benedict of Auxerre and one of the largest abbey churches to survive from the Middle Ages. Its 15th-century Washington Window shows the arms of George Washington's ancestors.

name: Selby Toll Bridge
text: Your train passes near Selby Toll Bridge, on the train's {side}, a swing bridge carrying the A19 over the River Ouse. The first bridge here, of timber, was built in 1792 to replace a ferry run by the monks of Selby Abbey since at least the 13th century, and is believed to be the first bridge in the world to use ball-bearings.

name: St Mary's Church, South Milford
text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church, on the train's {side}, built in 1846 in the Gothic Revival style to a design by George Fowler Jones, at a cost of £1,900 paid by the Gascoignes and the Church Building Society. Built for 300 worshippers, it became a parish of its own in 1859.

name: Conisbrough Castle
text: Your train passes near Conisbrough Castle, on the train's {side}, first built in the 11th century by William de Warenne after the Norman Conquest. Hamelin Plantagenet, Henry II's illegitimate brother, and his son rebuilt it in stone, with its tall keep, and Sir Walter Scott used it in his 1819 novel Ivanhoe.
